models.best: Inferred from its principle that status and alliances are built by giving, a candidate's standing rests on visible generosity and on the loyalty it returns, so support is earned through exchange and reciprocity rather than through price. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a gift creates an obligation to return, a donor's favour can later be called in as a vote, and a gift that is never written down leaves no public trace of who backed a candidate. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mauss, The Gift

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a household weighs its own labour against its needs, a local candidate can be backed by neighbours' labour and produce rather than by outside money. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production serves household consumption, a family with little surplus cannot spare time or money for campaigns, for travel to a count, or for a challenge to a result, so the poorest households have the weakest voice in choosing and contesting candidates. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that officials are paid from a common store, an office holder's pay comes from public stores rather than from private backers, so no candidate needs a private donor to take office. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the centre collects goods and allocates them by rank, the officials who hold the stores can reward supporters and withhold from rivals, so candidacy and votes can turn on access to the centre's allocations. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation

models.best: Inferred from its principle that output is sold through trade, owners who control labour and property have steady income to fund their own candidates, and the rules that protect their holdings are fixed in their favour. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that labour is extracted through ownership of people and the enslaved are denied education and property, the enslaved have no money to fund a candidate and no schooling to take part in a contest, so political choice rests with the owners. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a lord gives protection and justice in return for service, disputes over local office are settled within the manor, close to those affected, by people who know the land. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that services are owed to a lord, the lord controls who holds local office and hears disputes over it, so tenants who owe service have no route to contest a choice their lord has made. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that statutes fix entry, training and quality, the rules for choosing guild officers are written and known in advance, so a dispute over office can be settled by the statutes rather than by private favour. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that masters control entry, a closed body of masters decides who may stand for office and who may vote, so journeymen and apprentices who follow the statutes still have no say in choosing their leaders. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Epstein, Freedom and Growth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state regulates trade for national gain, customs and monopoly revenue fund the state's officials directly, so office does not depend on money raised from private donors for a campaign. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state regulates trade toward national gain, monopoly charters go to favoured merchants who can then back the candidates who grant them, so trade privileges and political support go together. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Heckscher, Mercantilism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a single tax on the rent of land funds the state, the cost of public office falls on one clear source that is simple to collect and easy to audit. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture creates a net product and land rent funds the state, the landowners who pay the tax have the largest stake in government, so they can finance the candidates who represent them while tenants and labourers have little say. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state protects property and contracts and otherwise stays out, candidates can raise money from willing donors on agreed terms, and disputes over those terms are settled by fixed rules. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state stays out of markets, the wealthiest donors can buy the most advertising and access, and a state that does little to restrain them offers no equal chance to candidates with less money. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Smith, The Wealth of Nations

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge held by many people, open competition among candidates and free donations let voters compare many rivals rather than choose from one approved list. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that state planning and credit expansion distort what is produced, a government that grants money or credit to favoured groups before an election gains support at a cost that voters do not see at the time. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society

models.best: Buckley v. Valeo and Citizens United: the 1976 ruling in Buckley struck down ceilings on candidate, independent and self-funded spending, except caps for candidates who voluntarily accepted public financing, and kept disclosure rules. These are summaries, not the opinions, and the link to this model is an inference, since the rulings rest on free speech rather than economic doctrine.
models.worst: Buckley v. Valeo and Citizens United: Citizens United (2010) widened First Amendment protection for independent political spending by corporations and unions, and discarded the part of McConnell that let lawmakers ban corporate independent spending. These are summaries, not the opinions, the McConnell point comes from a summary, and the link to this model is an inference. Source: National Conference of State Legislatures page on campaign finance and the Supreme Court (year not shown); online encyclopaedia (secondary), Britannica entry on Buckley v. Valeo; Public Integrity case profile (its Citizens United series)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public spending rises in slumps and falls in booms, a government's funds for parties and public office stay steady across the cycle, so office does not depend on donors whose money rises and falls with the economy. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the government in office manages the timing of spending and taxes, incumbents can time spending that voters see before an election, so a government may gain votes from public money that others pay for later. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Beveridge, Social Insurance and Allied Services

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a legal order curbs monopoly and gives workers a voice in firms, rules on party and corporate money can be set in law and applied equally to large firms. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: The Flick gifts and party donation disclosure: gifts from the Flick group to several West German parties set off a scandal in the early 1980s. Otto Lambsdorff, the economy minister, admitted at a parliamentary hearing that as a local FDP treasurer in the 1970s he had left Flick gifts off the public record, although the law required disclosure, and he described this as routine for parties. All sources are news reports, the excerpts do not tie each statement to one article, and the link to this model is an inference. Source: Christian Science Monitor news reports of 1984 and 1986 on the Flick affair

models.best: State subsidies to Swedish parties: a 1968 survey places their parliamentary approval in 1965, which puts public money into party funding. Only the approval year is given, from a summary, and the link to this model is an inference.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that services are paid by high taxes and that strong unions bargain nationally, a governing party with union backing has a steady base of members' votes and dues, which can make it harder for newcomers to compete for funds and seats. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Saltsjöbaden Agreement

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state sets targets for chosen industries and disciplines firms by performance, the government's programme is stated in public and judged at the next election by measured results, so candidates answer for what they promised. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state picks industries and directs credit to them, firms that depend on state credit have an interest in the government in office, so they may fund the party that picks them, and rivals outside the chosen sectors can be shut out of both credit and campaign support. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle

models.best: Inferred from its principle that land rent pays for public services, the public costs of office can be met from a tax on land value rather than from taxes on labour and capital. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that land value rises with public works and zoning decisions, owners of valuable land gain most from government choices, so they have strong reason to fund candidates who resist any tax on land values. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George, Progress and Poverty

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities are planned associations built by example, members of each community choose their own leaders and share the costs of common life, so candidates answer to people who can see their work. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that communities are built by example and planned in advance, a founder's plan can settle who leads and who may stand, so members who disagree have little route to contest the leadership or the count. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel

models.best: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit lets workers keep the value of their work, a campaign can borrow at cost from its own supporters rather than from a bank that charges more than cost, so no lender holds a claim over the candidate. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that free contracts govern all dealings, gifts and loans to a campaign are private contracts with no set limit, so a candidate who can lend or give the most can bind supporters to repay in votes. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property?

models.best: Inferred from its principle that members own and control firms and banks on the basis of one member one vote, board seats are contested in open member ballots where each vote counts equally, so no large investor can buy control. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that members share the surplus between users and workers, a few active or large-membership groups can dominate nominations and ballots, so newer or less active members may have little say in who is chosen. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mondragón cooperatives

models.best: Recall and pay caps in the Paris Commune: councillors could be recalled at any time and their pay was capped at an ordinary worker's wage, according to a movement-linked history site, not an independent history. The excerpt does not show which page states these rules, and no result says who could vote, so the franchise is not claimed here.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no state and free association replaces contracts, nothing sets how candidates are chosen, how votes are counted or how a dispute over a result is settled, so the most organised group in a commune decides. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread

models.best: Union political levy and the Osborne Judgment: members could opt out of the levy without being expelled for doing so, after 1913 legislation gave unions a legal footing for political funds. The opt-out wording is a summary from a secondary encyclopaedia entry, not the statute text, and no levy amounts or membership figures are given.
models.worst: Union political levy and the Osborne Judgment: a 1909 House of Lords ruling, the Osborne Judgment, made the levy that funded Labour through affiliated unions unlawful, and legislation in 1913 later gave unions a legal footing for political funds. The source is a secondary encyclopaedia entry, and no levy amounts or membership figures are given. Source: online encyclopaedia (secondary), entry on the Osborne Judgment (year not shown)

models.best: Union political levy and the Osborne Judgment: 1913 legislation gave unions a legal footing for political funds, and members could opt out without being expelled, which suits a route to socialism by democratic means. The opt-out wording is a summary, not the statute text, and comes from a secondary encyclopaedia entry.
models.worst: Union political levy and the Osborne Judgment: Labour's funding rested on levies collected through affiliated unions until a 1909 House of Lords ruling, the Osborne Judgment, made them unlawful, so the party's money depended on one legal channel that a court could close. The source is a secondary encyclopaedia entry with no levy amounts or membership figures. Source: online encyclopaedia (secondary), entry on the Osborne Judgment (year not shown)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control of industry through guild-like councils, the people who run an industry are chosen by those who work in it and use its goods, so leaders answer to a direct count of those affected. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state is only one partner among several in the councils, a council can be dominated by whichever partner has the most members or money, so a few large bodies may choose the candidates while the other workers have less voice. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole, Self-Government in Industry

models.best: Inferred from its principle that central plans set output and investment, campaigns and public office are paid from the plan rather than from private donors, so no candidate depends on wealthy backers. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: One candidate per district in the 1937 Soviet election: a 2020 academic article contends that the vote set a lasting pattern of one unopposed nominee per district, put forward under tight party supervision. A US embassy analysis speculated about motive, and a partisan paper forecast that 99% of districts would have one name, but the actual share is not given. Source: 2020 academic article (PDF; title and author not shown); US embassy analysis of the period (US government archive, 1933 to 1939 documents); Socialist Appeal, Trotskyist paper (1937)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices guide enterprises and a central board sets the rules, funding rules for candidates are fixed in advance and apply to every party alike, so no candidate gains from discretionary favour. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central board sets the rules and controls the investment, the board can steer public money toward the candidates who favour its investment choices, so state-owned firms and their managers may be drawn into campaigns they should keep out of. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Yugoslav workers' self-management

models.best: Recall and pay caps in the Paris Commune: councillors could be recalled at any time and their pay was capped at an ordinary worker's wage, according to a movement-linked history site, not an independent history. The excerpt does not show which page states these rules, and no result says who could vote, so the franchise is not claimed here.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state withers away only once classes disappear, the state that governs in the meantime controls candidacy and counting, and the principle sets no limit on that control and no route to contest it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme

models.best: Village committee elections under the Organic Law: the 1998 revision moved candidate nomination away from village groups and Party branches toward voters, and Article 14 requires more candidates than open seats, in translation. Monitors from abroad generally rated the votes they saw as fair, a secondary point not tied to a named source, and an East Asia Forum analysis argues the law partly shifts oversight of village leaders onto residents.
models.worst: Village committee elections under the Organic Law: official estimates put the share of contests with serious procedural flaws at about one third, and perhaps one village in four had fully met the statute's standards by late 2002. These flaw and one-in-four figures are secondary and not tied to a named source. Source: Organic Law of the Villagers' Committees of the People's Republic of China, Chinese and English text, 1998 revision; Carter Center report on China's village elections (1999); East Asia Forum analysis (2017)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' and consumers' councils plan through repeated proposals, every proposal is put to those affected and revised in turn, so no single authority sets the agenda for public choices. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that councils plan through repeated proposals, the body that drafts the first proposal can keep control of the agenda, and nothing in the principle gives a neutral body the job of counting or contesting the outcome. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward

models.best: Inferred from its principle that employers and unions are organised into state-controlled corporations, each trade has a recognised body that chooses its representatives, so producers have a set route for putting forward their own candidates. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Italy's Acerbo law and the 1924 election: the 1923 law gave two-thirds of the Chamber's seats to the list placing first if it won a quarter of valid votes, and after opposition walkouts in June 1924, accounts say intimidation and fraud helped. A 1928 overhaul replaced contested voting with a single slate picked by the Fascist Grand Council. Intimidation is a glossary summary, not a finding, the mechanism is unconfirmed against the law text, and the link to this model is an inference. Source: Verfassungsblog essay of 28 November 2023; online encyclopaedia (secondary) on the Acerbo law; IB revision-guide website (secondary; year not shown)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that finance shares profit and risk and that trust underpins contracts, supporters who fund a campaign share its risk, and no candidate owes fixed interest to a lender. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that trust underpins contracts, a candidate trusted by a close community may need no written rules for funding, so gifts and promises stay private and are hard for voters or rivals to test. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic life serves well-being and production is small-scale and local, a campaign can rely on many small local gifts, so no single donor or firm can carry a candidate. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that consumption is moderate and production stays small, local groups with little money may be unable to fund a candidate or a challenge to a count, so politics is left to those with larger means and the local voice is thin. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful

models.best: Inferred from its principle that property is widely held and decisions stay with the smallest competent body, funds for a campaign come from many small owners and offices are filled close to home, so no single large donor carries a candidate. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a just wage and widespread property are the aims, the small communities that subsidiarity leaves in charge can be run by a few local figures with little check from above, and a campaign can rest on local ties rather than on open contests. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Belloc, The Servile State

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic activity stays within planetary limits and a social floor covers everyone, campaign promises are judged against shared limits rather than against growth that donors want. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that limits are set for planetary reasons, incumbents can defend a limit that protects their own position and deny challengers a platform for growth, so the choice of candidates narrows to those who accept the existing limit. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Raworth, Doughnut Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that every citizen receives an unconditional income, poor voters depend less on donors and employers for a living, so their votes and small donations carry more weight in campaigns. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that taxes on land and natural resources pay for the income, owners of land and resources have strong reason to fund candidates who will set the rate and the rules for collecting it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government which issues its own currency is not limited by borrowing, funds for public office and public campaign finance can be set by vote rather than by bond markets or private lenders. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that inflation, not debt, is the real limit, a government can spend freely before an election and leave the cost to show up later as inflation that others bear, so incumbents may gain votes from spending that is paid for later. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a community sharing a resource designs, monitors and enforces its own rules, the people who choose local leaders can also watch how those leaders are chosen and funded, and disputes are settled under rules the community nests within wider institutions. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a shared resource is governed by rules designed by those who use it, the users who write the rules can exclude outsiders from choosing who holds the commons, so people from outside the community have no say in candidacy or funding for it. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons

compromise.summary: Open nomination with more candidates than seats, recall and pay caps for elected officials, public funding for parties with full disclosure of gifts, no ceiling on self-funded spending by individuals, caps and disclosure for independent spending by firms and unions, and vote counts observed by independent monitors.
compromise.details: Keeps: open nomination with more candidates than seats and observed counts (Chinese market socialism, Village committee elections under the Organic Law); recall and pay caps (Marxian communism and Anarcho-communism, Recall and pay caps in the Paris Commune); public subsidies to parties (Nordic social democracy, State subsidies to Swedish parties); no ceiling on self-funded spending (Monetarist neoliberalism, Buckley v. Valeo and Citizens United). Blocks: single-name ballots (Command socialism), by requiring more candidates than seats; seat bonuses (Corporatism and fascist economics), by proportional allocation; undisclosed gifts (Social market economy), by publishing every gift; corporate and union independent spending (Monetarist neoliberalism), by a cap and disclosure. Test: over two full election cycles, measure seats with two or more candidates, money from individuals against firms and unions, gifts found undisclosed by audit, and counts with complaints that monitors confirm. Source: Organic Law text (1998); Carter Center report (1999); Libcom Paris Commune article; Swedish party-finance survey (1968); National Conference of State Legislatures page; Flick affair news reports (1984 and 1986); Acerbo law essay (2023); 1937 Soviet election article (2020).
